title: Fulfillment status design review
summary: The whole review on one page: why the change, the tables as they are, the migration, the worker that writes the flag, and the report that reads it. Every block type in series.

blocks.title: Summary
blocks.text:
`orders.shipped` and `orders.status` disagree in about **0.4%** of rows, enough to put cancelled orders in the VIP report and to hide shipped ones from the warehouse dashboard. This page proposes one typed column, `fulfillment_status`, shows the migration that gets there without a long lock, and walks the two code paths that have to change.

Read top to bottom, or jump with the navigation. Comment on any section, or select words and comment on those. The questions at the end are the decisions I need from you.

tables.name: customers
tables.purpose: One row per account that can place an order. Guest checkouts get a row too, flagged by `is_guest`.

columns.name: email
columns.purpose: Login and notification address. Case-insensitive via citext.

tables.name: orders
tables.purpose: A checkout that reached payment. Status moves `pending → paid → shipped → delivered`, or to `cancelled` from pending or paid.

columns.name: status
columns.purpose: Free text today; a check constraint limits it to five values. See the proposed change.

columns.name: shipped
columns.purpose: Legacy flag, set by the warehouse job. Redundant with `status` once status is reliable.

columns.name: total_cents
columns.purpose: Sum of item line totals at checkout time, in minor units. Not recomputed later.

notes: `total_cents` can disagree with the sum of `order_items` after a partial refund. Refunds are recorded elsewhere.

tables.name: order_items
tables.purpose: Line items. Price is copied from the product at checkout, so later catalog changes do not alter history.

indexes.name: order_items_order_id_idx
indexes.purpose: Expanding an order into its lines.

tables.name: products
tables.purpose: The catalog. Soft-deleted via `retired_at` so historical order items keep resolving.

blocks.title: What goes wrong
blocks.text:
The warehouse job sets `shipped = true` when a label prints. Cancellation sets `status = 'cancelled'` and leaves the flag alone. A cancelled-after-label order is therefore both shipped and cancelled, and every consumer picks one:

- The VIP report trusts `status`, so the order counts as revenue.
- The warehouse dashboard trusts `shipped`, so it is hidden.
- Support sees both and asks engineering.

Two sources of truth is the bug; the fix is one column with the precedence written down.

operations.title: Create the enum type
operations.detail: A Postgres enum. Adding a value later is `ALTER TYPE ... ADD VALUE`, which is online but cannot run inside a transaction block before Postgres 12. Removing a value is not supported; that is the cost of an enum over a lookup table.

operations.title: Add the column, nullable, no default
operations.code:
ALTER TABLE orders
  ADD COLUMN fulfillment_status fulfillment_status;
operations.before:
status        text    not null default 'pending'
shipped       boolean not null default false
operations.after:
status             text               not null default 'pending'
shipped            boolean            not null default false
fulfillment_status fulfillment_status null
operations.detail:
Adding a nullable column with no default is a catalog-only change: the lock is `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` but held for microseconds, no rewrite.

A `NOT NULL` or a non-constant default here would rewrite the table. The constraint comes later, after the backfill.
operations.locks: ACCESS EXCLUSIVE for the catalog update only; waits behind long-running transactions, so run with `lock_timeout = '2s'` and retry.
operations.rollback: ALTER TABLE orders DROP COLUMN fulfillment_status;

operations.title: Backfill in batches of 10k by id
operations.code:
UPDATE orders
SET fulfillment_status = CASE
  WHEN status = 'cancelled' THEN 'cancelled'
  WHEN shipped AND status = 'delivered' THEN 'delivered'
  WHEN shipped THEN 'shipped'
  ELSE status::fulfillment_status
END
WHERE id BETWEEN $1 AND $1 + 9999
  AND fulfillment_status IS NULL;
operations.detail:
Run from a script that walks `id` in 10k steps with a short sleep between batches. Each batch touches one index range, holds row locks only, and commits.

The `CASE` encodes the precedence: `cancelled` wins over the flag, and the flag promotes `shipped` only when status has not already moved past it. The application starts writing `fulfillment_status` on every insert and update **before** this runs, so the backfill only has to cover old rows; the `IS NULL` guard makes it safe to re-run.
operations.locks: Row locks per batch. Bloat from ~3.1M updated rows; autovacuum handles it, or run a manual VACUUM after.
operations.rollback: Nothing to undo: dropping the column (op 2 rollback) discards the data.
warnings: Orders inserted between the column add and the application deploy will have NULL until the backfill reaches them. Verify with `SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE fulfillment_status IS NULL` before phase 2.

operations.title: Enforce NOT NULL without a full scan lock
operations.detail: The direct `SET NOT NULL` scans the table under `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE`. The four-statement form adds the check `NOT VALID` (instant), validates it under a `SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE` lock that allows writes, and then `SET NOT NULL` recognises the validated check and skips its own scan (Postgres 12+).
operations.locks: SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE during VALIDATE; brief ACCESS EXCLUSIVE for the other three statements.
operations.rollback: ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN fulfillment_status DROP NOT NULL;

operations.title: Drop the legacy flag
operations.code: ALTER TABLE orders DROP COLUMN shipped;
operations.before:
shipped            boolean            not null default false
fulfillment_status fulfillment_status not null
operations.detail: Catalog-only; the data stays on disk until rows are rewritten. Do this one release after the application stops reading `shipped`, so a rollback of the app does not meet a missing column.
operations.rollback: Re-add the column and recompute it from fulfillment_status: `shipped = fulfillment_status IN ('shipped','delivered')`. The original values are lost, but they are derivable.
warnings: Not reversible without a backfill. Search the codebase and dashboards for `shipped` before merging.

phases.title: Phase 1 · additive, this release
phases.detail: Deploy the app change that writes both columns, then run ops 1 to 4.

phases.title: Phase 2 · destructive, next release
phases.detail: After one release with no reader of `shipped`.

blocks.title: The writer
blocks.text: One code path writes the flag today. It becomes a status transition with the precedence from the migration's `CASE`, and it stops writing `shipped` one release before the column is dropped.

blocks.title: warehouse/mark-shipped.ts

steps.title: Load the order
steps.detail: Reads the row once. After the change this is also where the current `fulfillment_status` comes from, so the transition below can refuse an impossible move.

steps.title: Cancelled orders are left alone
steps.summary: The guard that the flag write bypasses today.
steps.detail: The guard exists, but it is checked **before** the label prints, and a cancellation that lands after it still gets the flag. With one column the write below becomes a transition `paid → shipped`, and `cancelled → shipped` is refused by the database, not by this line.
warnings: This is the race that produces the 0.4%.

steps.title: The flag write
steps.detail: Replace with `update(orderId, { fulfillment_status: 'shipped' })` guarded by `WHERE fulfillment_status = 'paid'`. Zero rows updated means the order moved on; return it unchanged and skip the event.

steps.title: The event
steps.summary: Unchanged, but only on a real transition.
steps.detail: Consumers of `order.shipped` today sometimes receive it for a cancelled order. Emitting only when the transition updated a row fixes that for free.

blocks.title: The reader
blocks.text: The VIP report is the consumer that matters most; it decides who gets the quarterly gift. Its status filter is the one line that changes.

blocks.title: reports/vip.sql
blocks.text:
WITH recent AS (
  SELECT o.customer_id,
         o.id AS order_id,
         o.total_cents
  FROM orders o
  WHERE o.placed_at >= now() - interval '90 days'
    AND o.status IN ('paid', 'shipped', 'delivered')
),
spend AS (
  SELECT customer_id,
         COUNT(*)         AS order_count,
         SUM(total_cents) AS spend_cents
  FROM recent
  GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT c.email,
       s.order_count,
       s.spend_cents,
       RANK() OVER (ORDER BY s.spend_cents DESC) AS spend_rank
FROM spend s
JOIN customers c ON c.id = s.customer_id
WHERE NOT c.is_guest
ORDER BY s.spend_cents DESC
LIMIT 100;

steps.title: Narrow orders to the last 90 days

anchor.exact:
WITH recent AS (
  SELECT o.customer_id,
         o.id AS order_id,
         o.total_cents
  FROM orders o
  WHERE o.placed_at >= now() - interval '90 days'
    AND o.status IN ('paid', 'shipped', 'delivered')
)

steps.summary: A CTE that keeps only recent, money-bearing orders.
steps.detail:
The CTE reads `orders` once and keeps three columns. Postgres 12+ inlines a single-reference CTE, so this behaves like a subquery, not a materialised temp table.

The date predicate is **sargable**: `placed_at >= <constant>` uses `orders_placed_at_idx` as a range scan. Writing it as `now() - placed_at <= interval '90 days'` would not.

cost.note: About 13% of orders fall in a 90-day window.

steps.title: Keep only orders that count as revenue
steps.detail:
`status` is free text with a check constraint, so the three literals must match exactly. If the proposed `fulfillment_status` enum lands, this becomes `o.status <> 'pending' AND o.status <> 'cancelled'` or a join to the status table.

The filter is applied after the index range scan, row by row. There is no index on `status` beyond the partial `pending` index, which this predicate cannot use.
warnings: A new status value added later will silently drop out of the report unless this list is updated.

steps.title: Aggregate spend per customer

anchor.exact:
spend AS (
  SELECT customer_id,
         COUNT(*)         AS order_count,
         SUM(total_cents) AS spend_cents
  FROM recent
  GROUP BY customer_id
)

steps.summary: One row per customer with order count and total.
steps.detail:
A hash aggregate over `recent`. `total_cents` is the checkout-time total, so refunds are **not** subtracted; see the open question on the schema page.

About 410k rows collapse to roughly 95k customers.

steps.title: Attach the customer's email

anchor.exact:
FROM spend s
JOIN customers c ON c.id = s.customer_id

steps.summary: Inner join to customers on the primary key.
steps.detail: The planner builds a hash on the smaller side. `spend` has ~95k rows and `customers` ~420k, so it hashes `spend` and probes it while scanning customers, or uses the pk index when the estimate is low. Either way this is cheap relative to the first step.

steps.title: Drop guest accounts
steps.detail: Applied after the join. Guests are about a third of customers but a smaller share of repeat spend, so this removes a modest number of rows. Pushing this into the CTE would require joining customers earlier and would not help.

steps.title: Rank by spend

anchor.exact: RANK() OVER (ORDER BY s.spend_cents DESC) AS spend_rank

steps.summary: Window function; ties share a rank.
steps.detail:
`RANK()` gives tied customers the same number and skips the next (1, 2, 2, 4). Use `DENSE_RANK()` for 1, 2, 2, 3 or `ROW_NUMBER()` for a strict ordering.

The window sorts all surviving rows by spend once. The final `ORDER BY` below uses the same key, so Postgres reuses that sort rather than sorting twice.

steps.title: Keep the top 100
steps.detail: Because the window function needs every row to compute ranks, the `LIMIT` cannot be pushed below it. The whole ranked set is built, then 100 rows are emitted. For a much larger customer base, a two-stage query (top-N by spend first, rank second) would avoid ranking rows that are thrown away.
warnings: LIMIT after RANK can cut a tie group in half: customers 99 and 100 may share a rank with customer 101, who is not shown.

blocks.title: Rollout and risk
blocks.text:
Phase 1 is additive and ships with the worker change in the same release; phase 2 drops `shipped` one release later, after a week of no reads. The backfill touches 3.1M rows in 10k batches and is safe to re-run.

The one thing I cannot verify from here is whether any dashboard outside this repo reads `shipped`. That is the last question below.

questions.prompt: Enum type or lookup table for the status set?

options.label: Postgres enum
options.detail: Compact, typed, no join. Values cannot be removed.

options.label: Lookup table with FK
options.detail: Values editable at runtime; one more join on hot paths.

questions.prompt: Backfill batch size and pacing. Pick what the write load tolerates.
Ties at the cut-off: which ranking semantics does the report want?

options.label: RANK() as written
options.detail: Ties share a rank; gaps follow.

options.label: DENSE_RANK()
options.detail: Ties share a rank; no gaps.

options.label: ROW_NUMBER() with a tie-break on customer id

questions.prompt: `orders.total_cents` drifts from line items after refunds. Where should the canonical total live?

options.label: Derive it in a view over order_items plus refunds
options.detail: No write path to keep in sync; a little slower on the account page.

options.label: Keep the column, maintain it with a trigger on refunds
options.detail: Fast reads; one more trigger to reason about.

options.label: Leave as is and document the drift
options.detail: Zero work now; reporting keeps special-casing it.

questions.prompt: Anything else that reads `orders.shipped` that the agent should know about before phase 2?
